indicators.note: 'without' in its old sense of 'outside', so one piece sits around the other

blocks.note: to shower things is to scatter them
a base or foundation, as in a bed of gravel
a shower is a brief fall of rain

explanation.surface: Someone dismisses a shower tray as a silly design, oddly mounted outside the shower itself.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shower' does two jobs with different senses: first a verb meaning strew, then a noun for a brief downpour. 'Without' is the old sense of outside.
explanation.definitionFit: A scatterbrained person is disorganised and forgetful, a fair synonym for foolish or daft behaviour.

clue.text: Bird seen around end of dawn chorus

indicators.note: to be seen around something is to surround it, so one piece encloses the other
the end of a word is its final letter, so only that one is kept

blocks.note: a chat is a small songbird, such as the stonechat
the final letter of dawn

explanation.surface: A birdwatcher hears a songbird joining in the dawn chorus.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dawn chorus' reads as a fixed phrase, but 'dawn' supplies a letter and 'chorus' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A chant is a phrase sung or shouted repeatedly in unison by a crowd, which is what a chorus does.

clue.text: Run-off that is in front of the wave

indicators.note: something placed in something else is enclosed by it
the front of a word is its first letter, so only that is kept

blocks.note: first letter of 'the'
i.e. is the abbreviation of id est, Latin for 'that is'
a breaker is a large wave crashing on the shore

explanation.surface: Water running off a beach just ahead of an incoming wave.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Run-off' suggests drained water, but here it is the extra contest that settles a tie. The abbreviation for 'that is' goes in after the T, then the wave follows.
explanation.definitionFit: A run-off is an extra race or vote held to decide a contest that ended level, exactly the job of a tiebreaker.

clue.text: Net profit is the aim of such business

definitions.text: Net profit is the aim of such business

blocks.clueFragment: Net profit is the aim of such business
blocks.note: surface reading: any company works to make profit after costs are deducted
setter's reading: the Net is the internet, so this business makes its profit online

explanation.walkthrough: 'Net profit' is a stock accounting phrase, which hides that 'Net' means the internet.
explanation.definitionFit: Trading conducted electronically over the internet is called by this name, so its profits are literally made on the Net.

blocks.note: a Bachelor of Arts is a graduate; 'post' says the next piece comes after it
to con is an old word meaning to study or learn by heart

explanation.surface: A thinker's further degree course after leaving university.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Postgraduate' must be split: 'post' tells you the study comes after the graduate. Francis Bacon was an English philosopher and statesman.
explanation.definitionFit: Francis Bacon, the Elizabethan thinker and essayist, is a famous example of a philosopher, credited with founding empirical scientific method.

clue.text: One charged with opening of night spots

indicators.note: something charged with a load is filled by it, so one piece goes inside
an opening is a beginning, so only the first letter is kept

blocks.note: an ace is the one in a pack of cards
first letter of night

explanation.surface: Someone accused of opening a string of late-night clubs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Night spots' looks like a phrase for clubs, but it splits: 'night' gives a letter and 'spots' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Acne is a skin condition producing pimples, so spots are its visible symptom and a common everyday name for it.

indicators.note: things misplaced are put in the wrong positions, so these letters move around

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A thinker who considered Buddhist moral teaching wrong-headed.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both wordplay and definition: 'He' is the man, and Friedrich Nietzsche famously rejected conventional moral systems.
explanation.definitionFit: The German philosopher challenged traditional morality, so describing him as someone who rejected an ethical system fits his reputation.

clue.text: Face full of sweat? Call for help

indicators.note: something full of a substance has it inside, so one piece is filled by another

blocks.note: dial is slang for the face, and a clock face is a dial
sweating is a sign of stress

explanation.surface: A sweaty, panicked face as someone shouts for assistance.
explanation.walkthrough: The face is the clock-face or slang sense, and the sweat is described rather than synonymised: perspiration is a symptom of stress.
explanation.definitionFit: A distress signal, such as a flare or mayday, is a message sent out to summon rescue in an emergency.

clue.text: Fancy attic’s rare in trendy property

indicators.note: fancy means elaborate or made up, so these letters are fashioned into a new order
one thing placed in another is surrounded by it

blocks.note: taken as written
chic means stylish or fashionable

explanation.surface: An estate agent's spiel: a fancy attic is rare in such a fashionable home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Property' suggests real estate, matching 'attic' and 'trendy', but it means a quality or trait.
explanation.definitionFit: A property in the abstract sense is a distinguishing quality or attribute of something, which is what a characteristic is.

blocks.note: surface reading: give up going on foreign holidays
setter's reading: travelling over the seas means sailing, so this is how a sailing ship halts

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests giving up foreign trips; the real sense is a ship travelling over the sea coming to a halt.
explanation.definitionFit: The nautical phrase means to bring a vessel to a standstill at sea by turning it into the wind.

indicators.note: one thing placed in another is surrounded by it

blocks.note: taken as written
a performer on stage is on
in heraldry a fess is an ordinary, a broad horizontal band across a shield

explanation.surface: A musician sings a piece in the key of C, nothing special.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ordinary' looks like 'plain', but it is a heraldic term: the ordinaries are the basic bold shapes on a coat of arms.
explanation.definitionFit: In criminal slang to sing is to inform or admit guilt to the police, so it means to own up.

clue.text: Wear me out in return for living in privacy

indicators.note: one thing placed in another is surrounded by it

blocks.note: to wear out is to tire, followed by me
rent is the return or income from letting property

explanation.surface: A complaint that a job will wear one out in exchange for a quiet life.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Return' looks like a reversal signal but here it is a noun meaning yield or income.
explanation.definitionFit: Retirement can mean seclusion or withdrawal from society, an old sense of a quiet secluded life away from company.

indicators.note: something placed around another thing encloses it

blocks.note: wheels is slang for a car
Zulu is the radio alphabet word for Z

explanation.surface: A tribal chief being driven around in a car.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Zulu leader' reads as a chief of the Zulu people, but Zulu just gives its letter and 'leader' stands alone.
explanation.definitionFit: A czar was the emperor of Russia, and the word is now also used for any appointed head of a policy area.

blocks.note: to sup is to drink
the press is the body of reporters
taken as written

explanation.surface: Choose: go for a drink with journalists, or gag them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Or' looks like a link offering a choice, but it supplies its own two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A censor stifles material by preventing its publication, so is someone who keeps information down and hidden.

indicators.note: to turn around is to face the opposite way, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: c is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for caught
slugs are bullets, and bullets are ammunition

explanation.surface: A butterfly is trapped in a garden crawling with slugs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Slugs' suggests garden pests, but they are bullets here.
explanation.definitionFit: The comma is a European species of butterfly named for the small white comma-shaped mark beneath its wings.

clue.text: Be on terms with struggling cook

indicators.note: something struggling is thrashing about, so these letters are thrown out of order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Get along well with a chef who is having a hard time.
explanation.walkthrough: Mrs Beeton wrote the famous Victorian Book of Household Management, the classic British cookery book.
explanation.definitionFit: Isabella Beeton is remembered as Britain's archetypal cookery writer, so she is a fair example of a famous cook.

indicators.note: something treated has been processed or worked on, so these letters are reworked

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A patient lashes out at a nurse who once looked after them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Kicks' reads as lashing out, but it is kicking a habit: giving something up.
explanation.definitionFit: To kick a habit is to give it up, and to renounce something is to formally abandon or forswear it.

blocks.note: nigh means nearly
tee is the spelt-out name of the letter T
a hole is a tight spot, an awkward situation

explanation.surface: A golfer's club almost on the tee by the hole.
explanation.walkthrough: The golf words mislead: 'club' is a place to dance and 'hole' is a predicament.
explanation.definitionFit: A nightspot is a nightclub or bar open late, which is the entertainment sense of club.

clue.text: Gamer’s bonus right on map before “good game”

blocks.note: on a conventionally oriented map, east is to the right
ere is a poetic word for before
GG is gamers' shorthand for good game

explanation.surface: A video gamer earns a reward for reaching the right spot on the map, then types the customary sign-off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Before' looks like a positional link but supplies the archaic ERE.
explanation.definitionFit: In video games an Easter egg is a hidden feature or secret message left by developers for players to discover.

blocks.note: first meaning: pillars that hold up a bridge or arch
second meaning: first name of the British TV presenter and journalist

explanation.surface: The fans who back a certain television personality.
explanation.walkthrough: Piers Morgan is a British television presenter and former tabloid newspaper editor.
explanation.definitionFit: Piers are the upright columns bearing a structure's weight, and the presenter's given name is spelt the same way.

indicators.note: 'of' marks what follows as the source the letters are taken from, here run across two words

blocks.note: the end of the first word runs into the start of the second

explanation.surface: Two or three wonderful moments.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A couple of' reads as 'two of', but 'A couple' is the definition: a romantic pair.
explanation.definitionFit: Two people in a romantic relationship are informally called an item, the same as being a couple.

clue.text: On-line clip of idiot — he’s quiet for one

blocks.note: a clot is a fool
taken as written
p is piano, the musical marking for quiet
e.g. means for example, i.e. for one

explanation.surface: A viral internet video of a fool, who happens to be a quiet type.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On-line' suggests the internet but means on a washing line.
explanation.definitionFit: A clothes peg is a small clip used to fasten wet laundry to a washing line to dry.

indicators.note: something that leaves goes away, so it is taken out of the word

blocks.note: an actor is a player
p is piano, the musical marking for quietly

explanation.surface: A movie star slips away from a set without fuss.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Film actor' reads as one phrase, but 'Film' is the definition in its sense of a thin coating.
explanation.definitionFit: A film of oil or dust is a thin covering spread over a surface, the same as a thin coat or sheet.

blocks.note: to play is to have fun
taken as written

explanation.surface: Enjoying yourself on the sand.
explanation.walkthrough: Playa is the Spanish word for beach, familiar from holiday resort names.
explanation.definitionFit: A playa is a sandy shore in Spanish-speaking countries, and also a dry lake bed in the American desert.

clue.text: Cuff that is small and round

blocks.note: S is the clothing-size abbreviation for small
a lap is one round of a track

explanation.surface: A shirt cuff described as little and circular.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cuff' looks like part of a sleeve, but it is a verb or noun for a blow; 'that is' merely links it to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A cuff is a blow with the open hand, especially to the head, which is the same as a smack.

blocks.note: a tot is a small child
an ally is a friend or supporter

explanation.surface: A youngster and a pal both chilled to the bone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stone cold' reads as freezing, but it is an intensifier, as in 'stone cold sober'.
explanation.definitionFit: Used as an intensifying adverb, stone cold means completely or utterly, as in stone cold sober or a stone cold classic.

clue.text: It is put into Italian food

definitions.text: It is put into Italian food

indicators.note: something put into another thing ends up inside it

blocks.note: pasta is the classic Italian staple
it is slang for sex appeal, abbreviated SA

explanation.surface: Something that goes into Italian cooking.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition too: passata, sieved tomato purée, is put into Italian dishes. 'It' meaning sex appeal is a crossword favourite.
explanation.definitionFit: Passata is strained tomato sauce used as a base ingredient in many Italian dishes such as pasta sauces.

indicators.note: to fool around is to mess about, so these letters are mucked about into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An interesting comic strip titled April Fools.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Intriguing' means fascinating on the surface but plotting here, and 'Fools' is a verb, not part of the April Fools' Day name.
explanation.definitionFit: To intrigue is to plot secretly, so an intriguing manner is a plotting, scheming one, like a conspirator's.
